conventions.convention: Real boxes are nonempty products of closed intervals with finite dyadic endpoints; degenerate sides are allowed and make the ambient interior empty.
Sturm variation deletes zero entries, and the root count is V(a)−V(b) on the open interval (a,b), with both endpoints nonroots.
The squarefree factors q_k label multiplicity k; constant input has no roots, while the zero polynomial receives a separate identically-zero status.
Scalar certification statuses apply to the original input interval, including after root-preserving contractions; exhausted budgets and non-finite evaluations give no absence certificate.
Krawczyk strict inclusion certifies existence; unique-root output additionally requires the outward row-sum bound q̄<1 and an exactly verified inverse witness WC=I.

Smooth isolation uses closed bisection halves; certified boxes may share an endpoint and need not represent distinct roots. Singleton contraction can certify a root at the original processed interval's endpoint.

load_bearing.statement: For finite real intervals on which the operation is defined, each finite result of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and squaring contains the exact set of values of the corresponding real operation; finite expression DAG evaluation preserves enclosure.

For C1 f on an open interval containing X=[a,b], a<b, with valid midpoint and derivative enclosures and 0∉D, every root in X belongs to N∩X. Empty intersection excludes roots; N⊂int X proves exactly one root in X.
For any x,y∈X, there is a point matrix A∈𝒥(X) such that F(x)−F(y)=A(x−y). The rows may come from different intermediate points.

For a C1 square map on an open convex domain, valid interval data and nonsingular C, every root in Y lies in K; disjointness excludes roots, strict inclusion proves existence, and q̄<1 proves at most one root in Y.
For nonzero rational P, the recursively defined q_k are monic, squarefree and pairwise coprime, P/lc(P)=∏q_k^k, and the roots of q_k are exactly the roots of P having multiplicity k.
For nonconstant P∈Q[x] with gcd(P,P′)=1 and a<b with P(a)P(b)≠0, the number of distinct real roots in (a,b) is V(a)−V(b).
For primitive squarefree integer P of degree d≥2 and height H≥1, every complex root has modulus at most R=1+H, and distinct roots are separated by at least H^(−(d−1))(2R)^(−(d(d−1)−2)/2).
For valid enclosures, each finite run terminates; excluded boxes contain no root, certified boxes contain exactly one root, and every initial root belongs to a certified or unresolved box.

alerts.finding: alg-validated-periodic-orbit-corrector admits a 'rational candidate box' Z and then instructs: 'run [[alg-krawczyk-root-certification]] on F and Z'. The called procedure requires an initial real box, and def-real-boxes-and-interval-jacobian-enclosures defines that box using 'finite dyadic endpoints'. Rational endpoints need not be dyadic: for example a period interval [1/3,2/3] satisfies the corrector's positive rational interval description but is outside the Krawczyk input domain. The corrector supplies neither a dyadic restriction nor a coordinate conversion before this call, so the call is unsupported for some admitted inputs.

seams_checked.note: Retained reading interface; the batch proves its certificates locally and does not substitute residual tolerance or ordinary Newton convergence for an exact root certificate.

Finite dyadic intervals, outward endpoint rounding, division away from zero and explicit non-finite statuses are preserved. The scalar mean-value applications satisfy continuity, differentiability and positive segment-length hypotheses.
Retained contextual interface; nonlinear Krawczyk existence and uniqueness are proved locally rather than inferred from a linear certificate.

The theorem correctly separates strict-inclusion existence from contraction-based uniqueness and uses the complete terminal partition. However, the corrector passes its generally rational candidate box directly to the dyadic-box Krawczyk procedure; see the alert.

The locator transforms physical time to dyadic local time [0,1], scales the derivative by the positive rational duration, supplies a positive rational width threshold, and handles unresolved outputs and duplicate endpoint roots explicitly. Its soundness theorem uses coverage rather than assuming certified boxes represent distinct roots.
